title: Dragonflies can live underwater for years, then fly for only a few weeks

cover.alt: A brown dragonfly nymph clings to a rough, weathered surface, just before the adult breaks out of its skin.

body: Most of a dragonfly's life is spent underwater as a nymph, breathing through gills inside its rear end and snatching prey with a hinged lower lip that shoots out from under its face. In large species the nymph stage lasts **up to five years**. When it is ready, the nymph climbs out of the water, its skin splits behind the head, and the adult crawls free and pumps haemolymph, its blood-like fluid, into its crumpled wings until they open out. Most species then live as flying adults for about five weeks or less.

slides.alt: A green and black dragonfly hauls itself out of its brown nymph skin, hangs from it, pulls its long abdomen free, and its folded wings slowly lengthen into clear, veined wings.
slides.caption: Time-lapse of a common clubtail emerging beside the River Thames: the adult pulls free of its nymph skin and its wings slowly expand. About 40 minutes pass in 24 seconds.

slides.heading: A long childhood, a short adulthood
slides.note: Upper limits: nymphs up to five years, adults of most species five weeks or less

slides.heading: Life as a nymph
slides.text: Nymphs moult between six and 15 times as they grow, depending on the species. Besides breathing through gills in the rectum, they can shoot forward by squirting water out of the anus, a handy escape.

slides.question: What does a newly emerged dragonfly pump into its wings to open them out?
slides.explanation: Pumping haemolymph into the crumpled wings makes them expand to full size. New adults are often pale and take a few days to get their full colours.
